copies.headline: Uncut Cokerr Does It Again, Obviously
copies.body:
Of course this is the grade. Adam spends round 1 on Jaxon Smith-Njigba at fair value, then treats the middle rounds like a heist. Kenneth Walker and Bucky Irving give him bell-cow equity at RB without ever reaching, Chris Olave and Rome Odunze fill in a receiver corps that's fine if unspectacular, and Sam LaPorta anchors a tight end room that becomes absurd once Mark Andrews falls into round 11 at plus-34 value. But the headline is Jayden Daniels sitting on the board until pick 79, a QB1 talent taken as QB12 money, then doubled up with Brock Purdy as a QB4 in round 12. That's not luck, that's a guy who does this every year.
The WR grade is the only blemish, thin after round 5 and leaning on Jalen Coker and Cyrus Allen as speculative dart throws. Doesn't matter. This is Adam being Adam — 34 and 22 for a reason, the guy who's never had a losing season and just keeps building rosters like the reigning champ he actually is.

copies.headline: The Aura Farm Grew Everything But Quarterback
copies.body:
Christian did the thing good drafters do: he let WR and RB come to him and refused to pay retail at quarterback, and it worked beautifully everywhere except quarterback. CeeDee Lamb at 11 is just clean value, then he backed it up with DeVonta Smith four rounds later at a plus-4 discount and stole Jameson Williams as a luxury WR4. Kittle at 86 is the headline heist of the entire draft, 20 slots below market for a top-five tight end. The RB room of Chase Brown, Etienne, and Tuten is legitimately deep, and Khalil Shakir for nothing in round 11 is the kind of pick that wins bye weeks. Deebo at 107 is the one swing that missed, paying 17 spots over market for a declining role player nobody else wanted.
Then there's the QB room: Trevor Lawrence and Jordan Love, a plus-value tandem on paper that still projects as replacement-level quarterbacking every single week. That's the tax on stacking elite skill talent, and it's very on-brand for the Aura Farm — spectacular ceiling, structurally boom-or-bust, exactly the profile that's gone 10-4 and 4-10 in back-to-back years. This roster can win a title or miss the playoffs from the quarterback position alone.

copies.headline: Rezac Finally Drafts Like He Means It
copies.body:
The running backs are the story here, and it's a good one: Saquon Barkley at 15 was already fair value, but grabbing Jeremiyah Love thirteen spots ahead of market in round 3 gives Logan a legitimate two-headed monster with upside neither of his previous title-curse rosters ever had. Add Dobbins and Allgeier as lottery tickets in the double-digit rounds and the RB room alone justifies the A. Justin Jefferson at 10 is just correct drafting, and letting Jalen Hurts fall to round 6 before scooping him nineteen picks late is the kind of patience that usually isn't in Logan's game. The WR room is fine, not great — McMillan and Burden are bets on unproven volume, and by the time you're relying on Pittman and Worthy for weekly points you're hoping health breaks your way.
Tight end is a dead zone, Isaiah Likely in round 9 a shrug more than a plan, but that's a punt, not a mistake. The real story is whether Logan can finally do something with a good roster in the playoffs. Two straight years he took the 1 seed into the postseason and left with nothing, then wore the dress for good measure in 2025. This team is built to get him back to that stage. What he does there is, as always, the actual question.

copies.headline: Burrowed Treasure Buries Its RB Room
copies.body:
CJ built this draft backwards and somehow made it work. The WR room is legitimately the best part of this roster: Rashee Rice, Emeka Egbuka, and a QB steal in Joe Burrow falling to round 6 give this team a real ceiling if the name Burrowed Treasure wants to actually mean something. But the running back room is a mess of reaches and hedges — Quinshon Judkins 17 spots early in round 3, then a parade of injury-prone or crowded backfields in Henderson, Hubbard, Pacheco, and Charbonnet. That's volume, not value, and it's why the RB grade sits at a D+ while everything else props the team up.
This is the same guy who's posted one winning season since 2022, so "boom-or-bust with a great WR corps and a shaky backfield" tracks with the CJ experience. If Burrow plays like a top-8 QB again and the RB dice land right, this is a playoff team. If not, it's another year below the line, just with better receivers to show for it.

copies.headline: All-In on Running Backs, Nothing Else
copies.body:
Noah did what Noah does: build a boring regular season and quietly stack a team that peaks when it matters. The RB room here is legitimately the best grade in this exercise, James Cook basically at cost and Achane falling to him nine slots late, then he doubled down with Stevenson as pure lottery-ticket depth. Problem is everything after round two got weird. Garrett Wilson and Mike Evans are fine but paid retail, Josh Downs at 89 is an actual reach nobody else was making, and the tight end room of Loveland-then-Strange is a wasteland — an F is generous if Loveland's rookie bumps don't show up week one.
This is very on-brand: nobody drafts Noah in round one of these grades either, and he's used to it. Five playoff wins and a title from the 7 seed says the process doesn't have to look pretty in August. The RB duo alone buys him a floor. Everything else needs the Achane magic to cover for it.

copies.headline: Isaac Built a Wide Receiver Museum
copies.body:
Chase at three is a fine start, but then Isaac apparently decided the receiver room needed to be load-bearing: Nabers, McLaurin, Metcalf, Wan'Dale, Meyers, Mitchell. That's six bodies at a position where he can start two, and it's why the WR grade reads F despite Chase being a legit top pick — hoarding is not the same as building. Meanwhile the backfield is Javonte Williams reached a full round early, salvaged by Skattebo actually landing where he should've in round 2. Bo Nix in round 10 forty spots ahead of ADP is the kind of panic move you make when you realize round nine just happened and you still don't have a quarterback.
The tight end room is genuinely his best work, Hockenson and Kincaid both banked as profit. But this is a roster built by a guy still chasing 11-3 in 2022, grabbing name value at one position like it'll refund the seasons since. Slap in the Face indeed — mostly self-inflicted, round 2 on.

copies.headline: Two Tight Ends, No Plan at Wide Receiver
copies.body:
John's namesake move here was punting the receiver room to build a two-headed tight end monster, and it shows: Brock Bowers and Trey McBride give him the best position in the league at TE, McBride actually a nice grab nine slots under market. Everywhere else the board fought him. Puka Nacua at 4 is just paying retail, Kyren Williams in round 4 is the one real coup of the draft, and then he spent the next eight rounds reaching for names he liked instead of value that was sitting there — Brian Thomas Jr. twenty-three spots early, Tyrone Tracy thirty spots early. That's not a draft strategy, that's nostalgia.
This is the John pattern in miniature: 6-3 on Peter for a reason, always finds a way to be dangerous by December even when August looks like a mess. The tight end premium plus Caleb Williams as a QB2 flier gives him a floor. But a D grade at receiver in a league this deep doesn't fix itself with vibes, and the ring hunt stays a hunt.

copies.headline: Gibbs Was the Plan, Then Mitchell Panicked
copies.body:
Jahmyr Gibbs at 1.1 is unimpeachable, and Nico Collins a round later is the kind of value that should set a draft's tone. Instead Mitchell spent the next fourteen rounds proving he doesn't trust his own board. Josh Jacobs eight spots early, DJ Moore seven early, Rachaad White reached by fifteen picks in round 9 for a committee back nobody wanted — that's not a strategy, that's flinching every time the clock hits ten seconds. Tyler Warren and Travis Kelce give this team an actual tight end plan, which is the one position he didn't overthink. Then he punted the quarterback position into a bonfire: Jaxson Dart and Daniel Jones as your only two arms is a bye week away from a scoreless Sunday.
This is peak Mitchell — never bad enough to bottom out, never sharp enough to matter, landing at 7-7 by some algebraic law of the universe. The coin flip keeps landing on its edge.

copies.headline: Lunchbox Built A Whole Skill-Position Ambulance
copies.body:
Leif spent this draft daring the RB position to hurt him, and it obliged immediately. Christian McCaffrey at 1.5 is fine on paper, terrifying in practice, and Derrick Henry in round two is a 32-year-old truck that's due for the wheels to fall off. Then it's David Montgomery, Woody Marks 28 spots ahead of his actual ADP, and Kaelon Black 40 spots early, which isn't a reach so much as a hostage situation. The TE room is Kyle Pitts and Greg Dulcich, which is to say the TE room doesn't exist. Meanwhile the WR corps — Adams, Marvin Harrison Jr., Diggs, Jayden Reed — is genuinely stacked, and grabbing Josh Allen 13 spots late in round three is the one moment of clean, cold value all night.
So the blueprint is: elite arm, loaded receivers, and a running back room built entirely out of injury history and wishful thinking. Vintage Lunchbox — 22-34 for a reason, always in love with the name over the medical chart. Basement's calling again.

copies.headline: Bijan Alone Can't Save The Basement
copies.body:
Peter's WR room is genuinely stacked. A.J. Brown and Tee Higgins came in three spots ahead of ADP each, George Pickens was fair value, and even Jalen McMillan and Jalen Nailor as lottery tickets late aren't crimes. The QB room is a heist: Lamar Jackson falling to round 5 is the best value on the entire board, and grabbing Dak Prescott as a QB2 in round 13 is pure luxury. But none of that matters when the RB room is Bijan Robinson and then a crater. Jonathon Brooks in round 7 was a 25-spot reach on a guy who might not touch the field early, Jordan Mason and Chris Rodriguez are bench fodder pretending to be a plan, and the TE spot never got addressed beyond a fringe Tucker Kraft flier.
This roster is Bijan or bust behind him, and byes will expose the whole operation by October. Peter's been chasing that 2022 high for three years now, and this draft has the same shape as the last two collapses — one league-winning stretch surrounded by nothing. The basement's still open for business.

copies.headline: The Diving Man Forgot How To Swim
copies.body:
Ashton Jeanty and Breece Hall at the top gives Kaleb a genuinely great running back room, the kind of thing that usually anchors a draft grade instead of getting buried by one. Everything else is where this goes off the rails. Drake London, Ladd McConkey, Carnell Tate, and Jordan Addison is four wideouts drafted like they were all going to be alphas, and none of them are, capped off by reaching for Addison 24 spots early like nobody told him the position was this deep. Then he panic-drafts two quarterbacks nobody needed, Herbert value be damned, and the tight end room is Harold Fannin and Kenyon Sadiq, which is a bye week disguised as a position group.
This is the same guy who won it all worst-to-first in 2023, and three straight 8-6 seasons since have apparently worn the magic off. The RBs will win him some Sundays. The rest of this roster is why he's 11 of 12 before Week 1 even kicks off.

copies.headline: Grant Built a Wheelchair Ramp to Nowhere
copies.body:
Amon-Ra at 6 is fine, unremarkable, the last correct decision Grant made all weekend. From there it's a fever dream of receivers picked ahead of their actual price tag — Zay Flowers ten slots early, Waddle four early, Christian Watson eleven early — like he was trying to corner the market on ankle injuries. Meanwhile the backfield got punted so hard it left the stadium: Jadarian Price, Tony Pollard, Jacory Croskey-Merritt at pick 91 for reasons known only to Grant, then Tank Bigsby a full 26 spots before anyone else wanted him. Kyler Murray and Baker Mayfield round out a QB room nobody drafted on purpose. Dallas Goedert 40 spots early actually pays off, which is the single joke of this entire draft.
This is peak Grant: 3-11, then 9-5, then whatever archaeological dig produces this roster. He didn't reach for names, he reached for vibes, and the vibes had a torn labrum. F is generous.

intro: Another Players Weekend, another draft that Adam Stockwell treated like a formality — Mr. Consistent walks away with the A+ again, because of course he does, the man is allergic to losing seasons and apparently also to bad boards. Christian wasn't far behind, but everyone else in the middle tier basically drafted to a shrug: solid-not-special from Logan, CJ and Noah, the kind of rosters that win you nothing at Players Weekend and nothing in December either. The real story is the bottom of the class — Leif, Peter, Kaleb and Grant all turned in drafts bad enough that someone in that group is measuring themselves for a dress in January. Fitting that Peter, still trying to live down the fastest title defense collapse in league history, can't even nail a Zoom draft anymore.
